feedback: If a learner relies on a single source: push them to find a second source and say what it adds or contradicts.
If a learner's recommendation ignores downsides: ask what the environmentalist (or the engineer) would raise against it, then revise.
Good justifications connect the choice to a named environmental effect, e.g. fossil-fuel CO₂ linked forward to climate change.
activities.intendedInsight: The 4-ESS3-1 practice is obtaining and combining information from multiple sources and weighing competing evidence to justify a position about resource use.
learnerActions: Take the role of an energy engineer, or hold a debate between an energy-company voice and an environmentalist, and gather information about a chosen energy source from more than one source of information.
Combine the information to describe how extracting and using that source affects the environment (for example fossil-fuel air pollution and CO₂, dam or mining habitat loss).
Justify a recommended resource choice by its environmental effects, acknowledging at least one downside of the option you favour.
activities.title: Obtain and combine: energy-engineer debate

feedback: If nuclear is sorted as renewable: fissile material is finite, so it is non-renewable even though a reactor emits little CO₂ during operation.
If electricity is listed as a resource: electricity is carried energy generated FROM a primary resource, not a resource itself.
If a learner equates renewable with 'zero impact': renewables are lower-carbon but still have footprints (land, materials, dam habitat loss, intermittency).
If a learner classifies by 'makes electricity': classification is about replenishment, not about what the source powers — both wind and coal can generate electricity.
activities.intendedInsight: Renewable/non-renewable is defined by whether the resource naturally replenishes on a human timescale, which is separate from how clean it is and separate from electricity (a carrier, not a resource).
learnerActions: Sort energy resources (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water) into renewable vs non-renewable using the replenishment criterion.
Match each resource to its characteristic environmental effect (e.g. burning fossil fuels → air pollution and CO₂; dams → habitat loss by flooding; surface mining → habitat loss).
Decide the two tricky classification cases: whether nuclear/fissile material is renewable, and whether electricity is a primary resource.
Given a new source not practised, classify it by whether it refills on a human timescale.
activities.title: Sort and match: renewable, non-renewable, and their impacts
